title: Magnetism and Electromagnetic Induction

cards.h: Electricity and magnetism are one thing
cards.b:
For centuries, electricity (amber and sparks) and magnetism (lodestones and compasses) looked like different subjects. Then, in the 1800s, experiments showed each makes the other. That discovery gave us electric motors, generators, transformers and eventually radio.

Almost all the electricity you use is produced by moving a magnet near a coil of wire.

Every magnet has a north and south pole. Like poles repel; unlike attract. Cut a magnet in half and you get two smaller magnets, never a single pole: no magnetic monopole has ever been found.

A magnet fills space with a magnetic field (B, measured in tesla), with lines running from north to south outside the magnet. A compass needle lines up with Earth's field because Earth itself acts like a giant magnet.

In 1820, Hans Christian Oersted noticed a compass needle swing when a wire nearby carried current. Moving charge creates a magnetic field.

A straight wire makes circular field lines around it. Wind the wire into a coil (a solenoid) and the fields add up, making a strong, bar-magnet-like field inside. Put in an iron core and you get an electromagnet, the heart of cranes, relays and bells.

cards.h: Magnetic force on charges and wires
cards.b:
A magnetic field pushes sideways on a moving charge, at right angles to both its motion and the field:

Magnetic force

F = q v B (charge moving at right angles to B)
F = B I L (wire of length L carrying current I)

Because the force is sideways, it makes charges move in circles. This bends particle beams in accelerators. The same force on a current-carrying coil makes it turn: that is an electric motor.

Michael Faraday asked in 1831: if current makes magnetism, can magnetism make current? Yes, but only when the field is changing. Push a magnet into a coil and a voltage appears.

Faraday's law

induced voltage = rate of change of magnetic flux (number of turns x B x area)

Faster motion, stronger magnet or more turns give more voltage. Joseph Henry in America found the same effect around the same time.

Heinrich Lenz showed that the induced current always opposes the change that causes it. This is conservation of energy: if it helped the change, you would get free energy. Push the magnet in and you feel a resistance; that effort is the energy you convert to electricity.

A generator spins a coil in a magnetic field, so the flux keeps changing and an alternating voltage appears. The spinning is done by steam, water, wind or diesel. A motor is the reverse: current in, spinning out.

A wire 0.5 m long carries 2 A in a field of 0.1 tesla at right angles.

F = B I L = 0.1 x 2 x 0.5 = 0.1 N.

For induction: a coil of 100 turns, with area 0.01 square metres, has flux in a 0.2 T field going from 0.2 x 0.01 x 100 to zero in 0.1 s. Voltage = (0.2 x 0.01 x 100) / 0.1 = 2 V. Spin it faster and the voltage rises.

• 'A steady magnet near a coil makes current.' Only a changing field does. A still magnet does nothing.
  • 'Magnetic force does work on charges.' The force is always sideways to the motion, so it changes direction but not speed.
  • 'Earth's north pole attracts the compass north.' The geographic north is near Earth's magnetic south pole; opposites attract.

cards.h: Thumba, the magnetic equator and the first rocket
cards.b:
The earth's magnetic equator passes close to Thiruvananthapuram. That is a main reason the Thumba Equatorial Rocket Launching Station was set up there, from where India's first sounding rocket was launched on 21 November 1963. Scientists studied the equatorial electrojet, a current in the upper atmosphere, using such rockets.

Nearly all of India's power, from hydro to thermal to wind, comes from generators working on Faraday's law.

• Moving charges create magnetic fields (Oersted, 1820).
  • A field exerts force F = qvB on charges, F = BIL on wires; motors use this.
  • A changing flux induces a voltage (Faraday, 1831); generators use this.
  • Lenz: the induced effect opposes the change.
